subtype: Approach: leaving the whole plan to the adults [Pitfall]
passage: Note from Charu, Kiran's mother. Two weeks before the holiday I asked Kiran what he would like to see. He shrugged, kept playing his game and said, "You decide." So the rest of us made the plan. On the second day, at the old stepwell, Kiran sat on a step and said it was boring; he wanted the model railway museum. It had never been on the list because he had never told us. He cried on the way to the next place, angry with us and, I think, a little with himself. That evening I asked him for one wish for the last day, and we changed the plan together. - Charu

qa.q: Where was Kiran when he said the day was boring?
qa.a: He was sitting on a step at the old stepwell.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling on the way to the next place?
qa.a: Angry and upset, with the family and perhaps a little with himself.

qa.q: What could Kiran have done before the trip, and why?
qa.a: Kiran could have named one thing he wanted to see, so it could be included in the plan from the start.

qa.q: How does Charu see what went wrong on the trip?
qa.a: Charu notices that Kiran's wishes were missing rather than that the plan was bad, so she invites him to add one for the last day.

grounding: A child leaves the trip plan to adults, and is upset when the places do not match his interests.

subtype: Approach: leaving the whole plan to the adults [Pitfall]
passage:
Tuesday, Hampi
Everyone's asleep and I'm writing by torchlight. Two weeks ago, when Usha-chithi asked, "Varun, what do you want to see in Hampi?" I said, "Anything," and went back to my game. Today was temples. Then more temples. Then a market with only brass lamps. I wanted the round basket-boat ride on the river that my friend told me about, but nobody knew I wanted it, so it wasn't in the plan. I sulked at lunch and Chithi asked what was wrong. I said "nothing" again. Now it's our last night. I think the only person I can be angry with is me.
Varun

qa.q: What did Varun want to do in Hampi?
qa.a: The round basket-boat ride on the river.

qa.q: How does Varun feel on the last night?
qa.a: Varun feels disappointed and a bit angry with himself for saying 'anything' when asked.

qa.q: What else could Varun have done when Usha-chithi asked two weeks ago?
qa.a: Varun could have named one thing, like the basket boats; even one wish gives the adults something to plan around.

qa.q: What might the trip have been like for Usha-chithi?
qa.a: She asked twice and still didn't know what Varun wanted, so she may have felt puzzled and a little hurt by the sulking.

grounding: A diary entry shows a child who left all the trip planning to adults and then felt unhappy that the places did not suit the child's interests.

subtype: Approach: leaving the whole plan to the adults [Pitfall]
passage: When the families on their lane in a village near Salem planned a day at the big fair in the next town, Parveen-akka, who organised everything, went to every house asking what each person wanted to see. Karthik was flying his kite. "Whatever. You decide," he called down from the roof. On the day, the list was the temple, the cloth stalls, a relative's house for lunch, and the cattle show. Karthik dragged his feet at every stop. He had wanted the giant wheel and the magic show tent, but by the time he mentioned them, the bus was leaving. On the way home he kicked the seat in front. His mother whispered, "Akka asked you, kanna." Karthik stared out of the window and said nothing.

qa.q: What was Karthik doing when Parveen-akka came round?
qa.a: He was flying his kite on the roof.

qa.q: What does Karthik kicking the seat suggest?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and let down, perhaps partly with himself for not speaking up.

qa.q: What could Karthik do before the next outing?
qa.a: Tell Parveen-akka one or two things he wants when she asks, so they can be fitted into the day.

qa.q: How might Parveen-akka see Karthik's sulking?
qa.a: She asked everyone so the day would be fair, so she may feel a little frustrated that he said 'whatever' and then was unhappy.

grounding: A boy ignores the chance to give his wishes for a family outing and ends up unhappy at places that do not interest him.
